edges.scope: Unsuccessful same-lab replication with weak control retention; cannot cleanly refute all reconsolidation
The cohort separately measured objective contact/participation and subjective loneliness; their weak association supports nonidentity, not independence.
The experiments treated being alone as a condition and measured affect separately; this supports the scoped condition/experience distinction, not a cure.
Acute deprivation prompted reported social craving in selected normally connected healthy adults; no diagnosis or chronic-loneliness intervention was tested.
Distinct daily need-satisfaction associations do not test substituting autonomy or competence for relatedness.
Group-level high-arousal affect results in one four-study undergraduate report; low-arousal findings varied and were not a treatment endpoint.

Specified empathy-focused calls versus no-call control improved UCLA loneliness after four weeks; another loneliness measure was nonsignificant and no statistically significant between-group change was detected on the social-network measure.
Eight-week guided internet CBT versus waitlist in a 73-person pilot; 61 loneliness post-assessments, without an active contact comparator.
Contextual synthesis reports heterogeneity and includes R48; it is not independent confirmation of the pilot, and granular bias tables remain unread.
Small piano-sequence experiment: similar measured TMS-map changes accompanied different performance gains; neither formal neural equivalence nor structural permanence was established.
Reported pooled estimate has acknowledged within-study effect dependence and partial access; not independent votes or a physical-practice percentage.
Different grasp/insertion task: imagery percentages are allocations of trials, not the meta-analysis estimate, a universal replacement rate, or support for another task’s result.
Combined practice improved an untrained finger sequence under unequal main-group training time; small additional volume control does not settle that explanation.
Explicit imagery versus response withholding in a 24-person sequence task; greater physical execution favored speed. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence.
Prose experiments reversed the restudy/retrieval ranking between immediate and delayed recall; no motor or social transfer measured.
Retrieval with feedback improved one-week prompted inference outcomes in small experiments; prompts signaled relevant knowledge and effect-size disclosure must remain attached.
Replication/extension using the original transfer materials retained a retrieval advantage but narrowed it with focused key information; time-on-task differed.
Narrative integrative review frames the performance/learning distinction; overlap with primary reports is not independent replication or new custom-method evidence.
Immediate classroom test/feeling divergence is a different outcome from delayed retention or inference transfer; no support for delayed benefits is inferred.
